extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, USPTO Office of Enrollment & Discipline, and counsel involved in USPTO disciplinary matters
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, rules, and procedures the USPTO applies when investigating, charging, settling, and sanctioning registered patent practitioners for misconduct (unauthorized practice, conflicts, communication failures, misleading OED, and related matters). Includes jurisdictional bases, specific regulatory violations, and included sanctions and reinstatement conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of practice before the Office (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice before the Office in patent matters includes preparing and prosecuting any patent application; consulting with or giving advice to a client in contemplation of filing a patent application or other document with the Office; drafting the specification or claims of a patent application; drafting an amendment or reply to a communication from the Office that may require written argument to establish patentability of a claimed invention; or drafting a reply to a communication from the Office regarding a patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order cites this definition to show that non-practitioner employees performing searches, drafting patentability opinions, drafting applications, and communicating with clients were engaging in 'practice before the Office.' Any activity falling within this definition may require a licensed practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO jurisdiction for disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director has jurisdiction over practitioner disciplinary matters pursuant to 35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32, and implementing regulations at 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.19, 11.20, and 11.26.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides the statutory and regulatory basis for OED investigations, complaints, settlement agreements, issuance of Final Orders, and publishing disciplinary actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5) — conduct prejudicial to administration of justice (pre-May 3, 2013)
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice by assisting in and facilitating unauthorized practice before the Office by non-practitioner employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assisting or facilitating unauthorized practice (e.g., allowing non-practitioners to perform patent work) can be cited as professional misconduct under the pre-2013 Code of Professional Responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.47(a) and (c) — aiding unauthorized practice (pre-May 3, 2013)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aiding a non-practitioner in unauthorized practice before the Office by maintaining a business relationship that resulted in a volume of applications only possible due to the non-practitioner employees' practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining or profiting from a business model that depends on non-practitioners performing regulated patent practice can constitute aiding unauthorized practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.62(a) — conflicts of interest (pre-May 3, 2013)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepting employment when the exercise of the practitioner's professional judgment on behalf of the client will be or reasonably may be affected by the practitioner's financial, business, property, or personal interests without obtaining consent after full disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referrals or business relationships that create a material risk of limiting professional judgment must be disclosed and consented to; failure to obtain written informed consent is misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.68(a)(1) — third-party compensation (pre-May 3, 2013)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepting compensation for patent legal services from a person other than the practitioner's client without obtaining consent from the client after full disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receiving payment from a third party (e.g., a referral service) for legal services requires client consent after full disclosure; nondisclosure is a sanctionable violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c) — neglect and client communication (pre-May 3, 2013)
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglecting a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner by failing to adequately communicate with clients about their intellectual property objectives, appropriateness of the type of patent application to be filed, Office actions received, and responses to be filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate communication about strategy and responses is part of competent representation; failure may be treated as neglectful representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(2) — reasonable consultation (post-May 3, 2013)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to reasonably consult with clients about the means by which the clients' objectives are to be accomplished, including communication about IP objectives, choice of application type, Office actions, and responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the Rules of Professional Conduct, practitioners must reasonably consult so clients understand how objectives will be pursued; lack of consultation supports discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(b) — explanation sufficient for informed decisions (post-May 3, 2013)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the clients to make informed decisions regarding the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must provide explanations sufficient for client decision-making about representation; inadequate explanation is professional misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.107(a)(2) — concurrent conflicts and written informed consent (post-May 3, 2013)
rubrics_metrics.description: Representing a client without obtaining informed consent, confirmed in writing, where there is a concurrent conflict of interest (e.g., significant risk that representation will be materially limited by financial or business relationships).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a concurrent conflict exists (such as heavy dependence on referrals from a related third party), the practitioner must obtain written informed consent after full disclosure; absence of such consent is a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.108(f) — third-party compensation (post-May 3, 2013)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepting compensation for representing a client from a person other than the practitioner’s client without obtaining consent from the client after full disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule reiterates that third-party payments for legal services require client consent after full disclosure, post-effective-date of the Rules of Professional Conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.505 — assisting unauthorized practice by non-practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Assisting non-practitioner employees of a third party in practicing before the Office in patent matters without authorization by continuing a business relationship made possible by their unauthorized practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting or enabling non-practitioners to perform regulated patent work, or relying on such a business model, can constitute assisting in unauthorized practice and is sanctionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b) — failure to cooperate with OED investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to cooperate with the Office of Enrollment and Discipline in an investigation, including by making misleading statements to OED.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners are required to cooperate with OED investigations; making materially misleading statements is a separate violation and aggravating factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d) — conduct prejudicial to administration of justice (post-May 3, 2013)
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice by assisting unauthorized practice by non-practitioner employees and by providing misleading information to OED during its investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule captures both aiding unauthorized practice and providing false/misleading information to disciplinary authorities as misconduct that undermines administration of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to disclose third-party payment/referral arrangements and obtain informed consent
rubrics_metrics.description: When clients pay a third party who then forwards funds to the practitioner (or when referrals generate most of a practitioner's business), the practitioner must disclose the arrangement and obtain the client's informed consent, confirmed in writing, including disclosure of amounts allocated to legal fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order emphasizes that lack of clear disclosure of payment flow and fee allocation, and failure to obtain written informed consent, are grounds for discipline under multiple rules (e.g., §§ 10.62, 10.68, 11.107, 11.108).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision and control over non-practitioner staff (avoid enabling unauthorized practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must supervise and control the role of non-practitioner employees to ensure they do not engage in practice before the Office; routinely allowing non-practitioners to perform patent searches, draft opinions, draft applications, and communicate with clients without practitioner oversight violates professional rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order treats routine unsupervised client-facing work and substantive patent tasks performed by non-practitioners as unauthorized practice and grounds for sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors considered in discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors considered include whether clients filed grievances, prior disciplinary history, and expressions of remorse; in this case: no client grievances, no disciplinary history (mitigating), but material misleading statements to OED (aggravating).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OED and the USPTO consider such factors when agreeing sanctions; lack of prior discipline and remorse may mitigate sanctions, while misleading OED aggravates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction: suspension from practice (36 months)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent is suspended from practice before the Office in patent matters for thirty-six (36) months commencing on the date the Final Order is signed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agreed-upon sanction for the listed violations in this matter is a 36-month suspension; the Order sets related conditions for reinstatement and probation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement eligibility and requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.60)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent shall be eligible to file a petition for reinstatement pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.60(b) thirty (30) months after the date of this Final Order; no petition shall be granted prior to thirty-six (36) months after the Final Order; OED may require a supplemental document compliant with 37 C.F.R. § 11.60(c)(3) asserting compliance with 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 during suspension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinstatement is governed by § 11.60 procedures, may require proof of compliance with corrective conditions, and OED has discretion to require additional documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition of reinstatement: CLE requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: As a condition of reinstatement, Respondent shall take at least three hours of Continuing Legal Education courses in which the primary subject is law office management and/or client communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeted CLE is required to address deficiencies in office management and client communication that contributed to the misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probationary period and enforcement mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent shall serve a twenty-four (24) month probationary period commencing on the date of reinstatement. If OED in good faith believes Respondent failed to comply during probation, OED may issue an Order to Show Cause with 15 days to respond and may request immediate suspension for up to one year from the USPTO Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order specifies procedural steps for addressing probationary violations, including transmission of materials to the USPTO Director and the potential for immediate suspension without waiting for further review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited recognition to facilitate compliance with § 11.58(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent is granted limited recognition to practice before the Office beginning on the date this Final Order is signed and expiring thirty (30) days after the date of this Final Order, solely for facilitating compliance with 37 C.F.R. § 11.58(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited recognition may be granted briefly to allow a suspended practitioner to handle narrow tasks needed to comply with suspension-related procedural requirements (e.g., notification, winding down matters), but it is time-limited and purpose-limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and notice of disciplinary action
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order in OED's FOIA Reading Room and publish a Notice of Suspension in the Official Gazette stating the practitioner, registration number, violations, and sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary settlements and Final Orders are publicly posted and summarized to inform the public and the bar of misconduct and sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of appellate/reconsideration rights in settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of the settlement, the Respondent agreed to waive rights to seek reconsideration under 37 C.F.R. § 11.56, to have the Final Order reviewed under 37 C.F.R. § 11.57, and to otherwise appeal or challenge the Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlement agreements often include waivers of procedural rights in exchange for agreed sanctions; practitioners should understand implications before agreeing.
